query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys (HEAs) initially frozen-in as a metastable multi-principal-element solid solution, isothermal annealing in the 300–600 °C range drives nanoscale precipitation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases (e.g. C14/C15 Laves or B2-ordered domains), which deplete Cr and Al from the matrix, disrupt the continuity of the passivating oxide scale, and thereby increase both aqueous corrosion rate and high-temperature oxidation weight gain relative to the as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, non-equilibrium metastable multi-element solid solution containing Mg, Al, Cr, Fe, Co, Ni (no detectable intermetallic by XRD).
generation.intervention: Isothermal annealing at 400 °C for 10–100 h (with controlled slow cooling) compared to retention in the as-cast state.
generation.conditions: Service-regime thermal exposures between 300 °C and 600 °C, static hold times from 1 h up to 100 h in inert and air environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates (Laves C14/C15 or B2-ordered domains) at grain boundaries and within grains.
generation.mechanism: Thermally activated interdiffusion and phase separation partition Mg, Al, Cr into intermetallics, depleting protective elements in the residual matrix, weakening the passive film and creating galvanic sites that accelerate corrosion and oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Annealed alloys will exhibit >5 vol% intermetallic precipitates, >2× higher corrosion current density, and >50% greater oxidation weight gain compared to as-cast.
generation.baseline: As-cast metastable solid solution exhibits <0.1 mA/cm2 corrosion current density and <1 mg/cm2 oxidation weight gain after 100 h at 600 °C.
generation.boundary: Above ~350 °C for ≥10 h, performance degrades sharply; below ~300 °C or <5 h hold, properties remain within ±10% of baseline.
generation.uncertainty: Exact threshold temperature/time and magnitude of performance loss depend on minor composition variations and grain-size effects; quantitative predictions are approximate.

falsification_experiment.design: Take twin sets of samples from the same as-cast HEA billet. Age one set at 400 °C for 50 h in air, cool identically to the other (control) set which remains unaged. Characterize both sets.
measurements: TEM imaging to quantify intermetallic precipitate volume fraction
XRD phase analysis for intermetallic identification
Potentiodynamic polarization for corrosion current density
Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) for oxidation weight gain at 600 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples show <1 vol% intermetallic precipitates by TEM and both corrosion current density and oxidation weight gain remain within ±10% of the as-cast controls, the hypothesis is falsified.
